This is a private complaint filed by the complainant against the accused for the offence punishable under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.

2. The brief facts of the complainant's case is as under:
It is contended that, the accused and her relative Lokanath are doing Saree and Gold jewells business and in this regard, for the improvement of business, in the first week of August 2018, the accused along with her relative Lokanath had approached the complainant and his wife for the financial assistance.

Considering the request, the complainant has handed over 220 gm of gold ornaments and Rs.1 Lakh in cash on 10.08.2018 to the accused on the assurance that, the accused shall repay the same within 8 months.

After the completion of the time agreed, when the C.C.No.24844/2019 complainant approached the accused for the repayment of the amount, the accused did not responded and thereby, the complainant's wife got filed a police complaint against the accused and her relative Lokanath on 15.05.2019 before the Nandini Layout Police station.

In the station, the accused and her relative Lokanath had requested the complainant and his wife to settle the dispute out of the station and agreed to return back Rs.8 lakhs towards the gold ornaments and the cash amount on 29.07.2019 and issued the cheque bearing no.408607, dt:
29.07.2019 for Rs.8 lakhs drawn on IDBI Bank, Gandhinagar branch, Bengaluru and also, executed the promissory note in favour of the complainant.

After the lapse of repayment date, when the complainant approached the complainant for the repayment, the accused assured to present the cheque assuring that, on its Mahesh vs Kavitha on 12 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144650937/
2 presentation, it would be honoured.

Thereby, the complainant has got issued the demand notice dt:06.08.2019 which was served on the accused, but she has not chosen to comply the demand, which has given cause of action to file the present complaint.
3. After filing of the complaint, this court has taken cognizance of the offence punishable U/s.138 of N.I.Act.
Sworn statement of the complainant was recorded.
Being satisfied that, there are prima-facie materials to proceed against accused, summons was issued.
After appearance of the accused, she was enlarged on bail and plea was recorded.
The accused has not pleaded guilty, but submitted that, he would go for the trial.

From the basis of the pleadings, the following points that arise for my consideration are as follows:-
1.

Whether the complainant proves that, the accused issued cheque bearing no.408607, dt: 29.07.2019 for Rs.8 lakhs drawn on IDBI Bank, Gandhinagar branch,
Bengaluru towards discharge of her legal liability which was returned unpaid on presentation for the reason " Account Blocked situation covered in 2125" and despite of knowledge of the notice, she has not paid the said cheque amounts and thereby,
committed an offence punishable U/s.138 of N.I.Act?

sentences.text: The complainant has filed this complaint alleging that, the accused has committed an offence punishable U/s.138 of N.I.Act.

He pleads and C.C.No.24844/2019 asserts that, the accused along with her relative Lokanath had approached him for the financial assistance for developing the Saree and Jewells business and thereby, he had handed over 220 gms of gold with cash of Rs.1 Lakh on the assurance that, the accused would repay the amount within 8 months.

As she failed to pay the amount, a complaint was lodged and out of the police station, the accused has issued the disputed cheque and also executed the promissory note assuring to present the cheque which is being dishonoured and thereby, he has issued the demand notice which is being served on the accused,
despite she has not chosen to comply the demand, which has given a cause of action to file the complaint.

10. In this scenario, if the documents placed by the complainant is scrutinized, the complainant in order to examine the compliance of statutory requirements as C.C.No.24844/2019 envisaged U/s.138 of NI Act, he got produced the Ex.P.1 the cheque dt:29.07.2019.

The said cheque is returned with an endorsement as Funds Insufficient as per Ex.P.2, the return advise dt: 31.07.2019, the Ex.P.3 is the office copy of the legal notice dt: 06.08.2019, Ex.P.4 are the postal receipts, Ex.P.5 & 6 are the served acknowledgment which indicates the service on 07.08.2019.
The present complaint is filed on 30.08.2019.
A careful scrutiny of the documents relied by the complainant goes to show that, a statutory requirement of Sec.138 of NI Act is being complied with and this complaint is filed well in time.
The complainant has discharged his initial burden by examining him as PW.1 and by producing the documents as referred above.

Thus, complainant is entitled to rely on the statutory presumptions enshrined U/s.118 R/w. Sec. 138 of N.I.Act.
C.C.No.24844/2019 Sec. 118 of the Act reads as thus, that every Negotiable Instrument was made or drawn for consideration and that, every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed,
negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration.
Further Sec.139 of Negotiable Instrument Act provides for presumption infavour of PA holder.

It reads like this, it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that, the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Sec. 138, for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or any other liability.

11. A combined reading of the referred sections raises a presumption infavour of the holder of the cheque that, he has received the same for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability.

No doubt, the said presumptions of law are rebuttable in nature, the accused C.C.No.24844/2019 can take probable defense in the scale of preponderance of probabilities to rebut the presumption available to the complainant.

It is need less to say that, the evidence of the PW.1 can be rebutted even by effectively cross-examining the PW.1, rather entering the witness box.
12.
So here, it is relevant to note that, whether the accused has really rebutted the presumption available under the law which requires due consideration.
It is an undisputed fact that, the disputed cheque at Ex.P.1 does belongs to the accused and also, the signature therein at Ex.P.1(a).

Even, the Mahesh vs Kavitha on 12 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144650937/
4 dishonour of the cheque at Ex.P.2 is not in dispute.

sentences.text: Even the issuance of demand notice at Ex.P.3 cannot be denied as the Ex.P.4 would reveal the issuance of demand notice, but however the accused disputes its service.

Here, the complainant claims that, the accused has raised loan and towards the discharge of the C.C.No.24844/2019 said liability, has issued the disputed cheque which is being seriously denied by the accused.
She has totally denied the receipt of the gold or the loan as claimed by the complainant and also, deny the issuance of the disputed cheque as claimed by the complainant.
She also denies the receipt of the demand notice.

So, in this back ground, if the rival claims of the parties are taken into consideration the burden would be upon the complainant to establish the loan transaction and the issuance of the disputed cheque toward the discharge of legally enforceable liability.
13. In this regard, the complainant has got filed his sworn statement which is being treated as evidence and as said, he has got produced 7 documents as per Ex.P.1 to 7.
As said, the disputed cheque belongs to the accused and its signature is not in dispute.
Perhaps, on perusal of Ex.P.1 it suffices that, the accused owns a shop called Aishwarya C.C.No.24844/2019 Jewelers, for which she is the proprietor.

Nowhere, the accused do deny her ownership over the Aishwarya Jewelry shop is concerned and also, nowhere she would deny the fact of she issuing the disputed cheque to the complainant, but disputes for issuing the legally recoverable debt.
So, the claim of the complainant that, the complainant is the proprietor of Aishwarya Jewellary to be accepted.

Here, it is relevant to note that, though the accused has not led her evidence by stepping the witness box or specifically pleading her defence while recording her acquisition, but the cross examination of the PW.1 would go to indicate that, she has taken a specific defence that, the disputed cheque was being taken in a police station by putting her in force.
So, here, it is also necessary to note that, as the accused was able to establish her defence which also requires due consideration.

Here, it is relevant to note that, the accused not only has admitted her signature in the disputed cheque at Ex.P.1, but has also admitted her signature in Ex.P.7 the promissory note, on which the complainant has placed his complete reliance so far the the loan transaction is concerned.

Because,
by placing Ex.P.7, the complainant has not only pleaded the accused handing over the disputed cheque by acknowledging the liability, but has also categorically deposed in his evidence about the accused issuing the disputed cheque towards the legal debt.

Here, it is relevant to note that, though the accused admit the signature appearing in Ex.P.7 belongs to her, but again in the cross examination of PW.1, she not only contends that, the signature in Ex.P.7 was taken through force in police station, but also has taken a defence that, her signature was taken in a blank stamp paper which is later on created C.C.No.24844/2019 by the complainant.

But absolutely, to appreciate the said defence, the accused has neither chosen to elicit the said fact from the mouth of the PW.1 or chosen to step into the witness box or chosen to place any probable evidence to appreciate the said defence.

Perhaps, while going through the cross examination of PW.1, it indicates that, though the accused has defended her case by taking a specific stand that, the disputed cheque at Ex.P.1 and the promissory note at Ex.P.7 were never issued and executed under free consent, but again there is no evidence forth coming to appreciate her defence.

Because when the accused was so particular that,
she was forced to issue the disputed cheque at Ex.P.1 and the promissory note at Ex.P.7, nothing had Mahesh vs Kavitha on 12 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144650937/
5 prevented her to refuse to sign and issue the documents or to initiate some legal action against the concerned police officers or the complainant at a particular point of time.
It is an admitted fact that, a police complaint was lodged by the complainant wife against the accused and her relative in the year 2019.

When, the police complaint is alleged to be filed in the year 2019 and the signature of the accused at Ex.P.1 & 7 alleged to be taken in the year 2019 under force, certainly nothing had prevented the accused to take some appropriate steps at a particular point of time, which admittedly not forthcoming.
Infact, the the accused could have instructed her bank to stop the payment of the disputed cheque by disclosing the real incident.

No doubt, the bank endorsement at Ex.P2 would reveal that, it is being dishonored with shara as Account blocked situation covered in 2125, but that shara is not clear as to whether it is being dishonored on the instruction given by the accused.
Nothing, had prevented the accused to get examined the bank witness to that regard.
Even nothing C.C.No.24844/2019 had prevented her to demand the return of the cheque in writing at a particular point of time.
This evidence would go to indicate that, the stand taken by the accused has no force.
16. So, in this back ground, the contents reduced in Ex.P.1 & P.7 has to be accepted.
If the contents reduced therein is acceptable, then it suffices that, the accused has issued the disputed cheque towards the legally enforceable liability which cannot be brushed aside.

No doubt, many questions were posed to the PW.1 with regard to his financial capacity in advancing Rs.1 Lakh and the gold ornaments of 220 gms and its receipts/documents and loan transaction not being disclosed in the I.T.returns, but the complainant has categorically deposed that, he was working as a Editor in Vijaya Karnataka Daily News paper and he is also earning as a LIC agent and he is also having C.C.No.24844/2019 a source from his agricultural land.

Though, no document is produced to this regard, but again when the accused utterly failed to elicit the answers in his favour, more particularly when her defence appears not to be proved, I am of the considered view that, the defence raised by the accused is only to avoid the liability under the disputed cheque.

Having, the complainant has established the Ex.P.1 and the Ex.P.7, the contents reduced therein requires to be accepted and this suffices that, the complainant has established the loan transaction and issuance of the cheque towards the legal liability.
17. The Ex.P.3 is the legal notice issued by the complainant demanding the payment of the cheque amount and it is being served as per Ex.P.5 & 6.
Here, the accused categorically denies the receipt of the notice questioning the signature appearing therein.
It is an admitted fact that, the C.C.No.24844/2019 signature appearing therein does not belongs to the accused, but nowhere the accused do deny the postal address referred therein.
When, the accused has admitted the fact of the postal address referred therein, it suffices that, the complainant has furnished the correct address of the accused.
Moreso, the accused has got appeared through the counsel on the court process being served on her.
When this fact is taken into consideration, it suffices that, even not replying the notice at the initial stage would give a serious doubt so far the defence case is concerned.

It could be said that, any stretch of denial from the defense that, the Ex.P.1 was not issued towards the legally recoverable debt cannot be accepted, when more particularly the accused has not chosen to reply the Mahesh vs Kavitha on 12 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144650937/
6 legal notice which is being served on the accused and this fact, goes to establish the C.C.No.24844/2019 issuance of the cheque by the accused was towards the discharge of the loan liability.
18. As said, the complainant has got issued the legal notice as per Ex.P.3 and it is being served upon the accused as per Ex.P.5 & 6.
Admittedly, no probable evidence are placed on record as to why she has not opted to reply the notice at the initial stage.

In the decision reported in 2019 SCC OnLine Kar.2117-V.R.Shresti Vs., Bhaskar.P., wherein the Hon'ble High court has opined that, if really the accused had no transaction with the complainant, he would have given reply to the notice and not replying the same would go to establish that, the defence made is false and the court should draw the presumption against the accused for not replying the legal notice.
The decision aptly applies to the case in hand.

Not replying the notice at the initial stage would hold no water so far the defence case is C.C.No.24844/2019 concerned and in this background, the case of the complainant has to be accepted by drawing presumption.
19.

In the decision reported in (2021) 5 SCC 283 - Kalamani Tex and Another., Vs.
P.Balasubramanian, (2010) 11 SCC 441- Rangappa Vs. Sri.Mohan., Wherein it is held that, when once the signature of an accused on the cheque is established, than the reverse onus clauses become operative, also aptly applies to the case in hand.

sentences.text: When the complainant has established the accused having issued the cheque at Ex.P.1 towards the discharge of legal liability and their existed a legally enforceable liability, the onus to disprove it, shifts on the accused which is not been proved by placing positive evidence.

In this background, having the accused not disputed the complainant case by placing positive evidence, I am of the considered view that, the cheques issued by the accused at Ex.P.1 is for the C.C.No.24844/2019 legally enforceable liability and this fact is being established by the complainant by placing cogent and positive evidence which is not rebutted by the other side.
20.
It is need less to say that, documentary evidence do prevail on the oral evidence.

Absolutely,
there is no evidence available on record, to hold that, the disputed cheque was obtained in station with force.

So, in this back ground when the provisions U/s.118 and 139 of N.I. Act is looked into, it raises the presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that, he has received the same for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability.
It also permits the complainant to fill the cheque having established the Ex.P.1 being issued towards the discharge of legal liability.
As said above, the accused has not disputed the cheque does pertains to her.
It could be said that, the accused has not disputed the cheque in question C.C.No.24844/2019 and signature found therein.
When the drawer has admitted the issuance of cheque as well as the signature present therein, the presumption envisaged U/s.118 R/w.139 of N.I.Act would operate infavour of the complainant.
The said provisions lies on a special rule of evidence applicable to negotiable instruments.
The presumption is one of law and thereunder the court shall presume that, the instrument was endorsed for consideration.
So also, in the absence of contrary evidence on behalf of the accused, the presumption U/s.118 of N.I.Act goes in favour of the complainant.

No doubt, as said statutory presumptions are rebuttable in nature, but when the complainant has relied upon the statutory presumptions enshrined U/s.118 R/w.Sec.139 of N.I.Act, it is for the accused to rebut the presumption with cogent and convincing evidence.

Mahesh vs Kavitha on 12 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144650937/
7 C.C.No.24844/2019 21.
It is worth to note that, Sec.106 of Indian Evidence Act postulates that, the burden is on the accused to establish the fact which is especially within its knowledge.
This provision is exception to the general rule that, the burden of proof is always on the prosecution to establish its case beyond all reasonable doubt.
In that view of matter, the burden is on the accused to prove that, the cheque in question was not issued for discharge of any liability.
But, despite the accused has taken the defence that, the Ex.P.1 was not issued towards the legal liability to the complainant, but the said fact and the version is not been established.
From the discussion made supra, it could be said that, the complainant has established his case by placing positive evidence.
On the other hand, the accused failed to establish her defence by placing probable defence and also, failed to elicit the said fact from the mouth of the C.C.No.24844/2019 PW.1.
In this back ground, the case of the complainant requires to be accepted.
The evidence placed on record establishes that, the complainant has proved that, for discharge of the legal liability, the accused has issued Ex.P.1 and it is being dishonored as per Ex.P.2.

Therefore, Point No.1 is answered in the "Affirmative'.
22. Point No.2:-
For the reasons discussed in the point No.1, the complainant has proved the guilt of the accused punishable U/s.138 of N.I.Act.

The Hon'ble Apex Court also dealt in the decision reported in (2018) 1 SCC 560, M/s. Meters and Instrument Pvt. Ltd., Vs. Kanchana Mehta., wherein It is held that "the object of provision being primarily compensatory, punitive element being mainly with the object of enforcing the compensatory element, compounding at the initial stage has to be encouraged, but is not debarred at the later stage subject to appropriate C.C.No.24844/2019 compensation has may be found acceptable to the parties or the court".

sentences.text:
By considering the decision,
it could be said that, the time when the transaction has taken place and the primary object of the provision being kept in mind, I am of the considered view that rather imposing punitive sentence, if sentence of fine is imposed with a direction to compensate the complainant for its monetary loss by awarding compensation with interest U/s.396 of BNSS 2023, it would meet the ends of justice.
By considering these aspects, I am of the considered view that, it would be just and proper to impose fine of Rs.8,05,000/-.
Out of the compensation of Rs.8,05,000/-, an amount of Rs.8,00,000/- shall be awarded to the complainant U/s.396 of BNSS 2023.

Accordingly I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER
Acting U/s.278(2) of BNSS -2023 (Old Correspondence No. 255(2) of Code of C.C.No.24844/2019 Criminal Procedure)

, the accused is convicted for the offence punishable under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the accused is sentenced to pay fine of Rs.8,05,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs and Five Thousand only)
.
In default thereof, the accused shall undergo simple imprisonment for the term of one year.
Acting U/s. 396 of BNSS - 2023 (Old  Correspondence No.357(1)(b) of Cr.P.C), it is ordered that, Rs.8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs only), there from shall be paid to the complainant as compensation.

8 Five Thousand only) is defrayed to the state for the expenses incurred in the prosecution.

In this background, having the accused not disputed the complainant case by placing positive evidence, I am of the considered view that, the cheques issued by the accused at Ex.P.1 is for the C.C.No.24844/2019 legally enforceable liability and this fact is being established by the complainant by placing cogent and positive evidence which is not rebutted by the other side.
20.
Absolutely,
there is no evidence available on record, to hold that, the disputed cheque was obtained in station with force.
When the drawer has admitted the issuance of cheque as well as the signature present therein, the presumption envisaged U/s.118 R/w.139 of N.I.Act would operate infavour of the complainant.
The said provisions lies on a special rule of evidence applicable to negotiable instruments.
The presumption is one of law and thereunder the court shall presume that, the instrument was endorsed for consideration.
So also, in the absence of contrary evidence on behalf of the accused, the presumption U/s.118 of N.I.Act goes in favour of the complainant.
No doubt, as said statutory presumptions are rebuttable in nature, but when the complainant has relied upon the statutory presumptions enshrined U/s.118 R/w.Sec.139 of N.I.Act, it is for the accused to rebut the presumption with cogent and convincing evidence.
It is worth to note that, Sec.106 of Indian Evidence Act postulates that, the burden is on the accused to establish the fact which is especially within its knowledge.
This provision is exception to the general rule that, the burden of proof is always on the prosecution to establish its case beyond all reasonable doubt.
But, despite the accused has taken the defence that, the Ex.P.1 was not issued towards the legal liability to the complainant, but the said fact and the version is not been established.
On the other hand, the accused failed to establish her defence by placing probable defence and also, failed to elicit the said fact from the mouth of the C.C.No.24844/2019 PW.1.
